newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Few signs of world backing for Afghan victors.
newsitem.headline: Few signs of world backing for Afghan victors.

text.p: Pakistan stood alone on Friday in signalling recognition of Afghanistan's new Taleban rulers after the Islamic militia seized the capital Kabul.

Islamabad's tepid welcome contrasted with dismay over the Taleban's execution of former Soviet-backed Afghan president Najibullah, who had been forced to hide in a UN compound in Kabul since he was toppled in 1992.
In Moscow, Mikhail Gorbachev condemned as a "lynching" the killing of Najibullah, the man installed as Afghan leader in 1987 during the Soviet occupation of the country.

Gorbachev, who was ousted from the Kremlin months before his protege's reign in Kabul was cut short in 1992, said Najibullah, a diehard communist dubbed the "Butcher of Kabul", had "understood the destructiveness for his country of the socialist path of development."
"This was a lynching and some sort of savagery," he said.
U.N. peace envoy for Afghanistan Norbert Holl voiced "deep dismay" at Najibullah's execution.

Holl, who heads the United Nations Special Mission to Afghanistan (USMA), said armed men abducted Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai from the USMA compound in Kabul in the early hours of Friday and later killed them.

He said the abduction of the former president and his companions and the subsequent killings "without any legitimate judicial procedure" constituted a grave violation of the immunity UNSMA premises enjoyed under international law.
"The taking of Kabul by the Talebans marks a new development in the conflict which has bloodied the country for four years," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters.
Asked about the killing of Najibullah, he answered: "We can only regret such a violent act."

Pakistan called for restraint and peace talks and said: "In keeping with its policy, the government of Pakistan will send immediately a delegation to establish contact with the new government in Kabul and maintain its contact with the Taleban Shura (council) in (the southern town of) Kandahar."
Other Asian governments were not so supportive.

"Japan has over a long time made exhaustive efforts to achieve a settlement of the Afghan situation, and hopes that all parties to the latest conflict refrain from fighting and return to the table for peaceful dialogue as soon as possible," Japan's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl said: "We are following the developments of the situation very carefully in Kabul and we hope that the situation will not further escalate for the sake of the innocent civilian victims."
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani called on Afghan factions to stop fighting and set up a joint administration in the neighbouring country.

"I wish to God that they come to their senses, stop fighting and let one person, one group, one party or an joint assembly make peace in the country," Rafsanjani said in a mass prayer sermon broadcast on Tehran radio.
Iran had supported the Kabul government as legitimate. It has been hostile to the Taleban, whom Iranian media accused of being manipulated by Pakistan and the United States.
But Iran's media appeared to have toned down their criticism of the Taleban in the past few weeks and Iranian officials have held talks with representatives of the militia.
